_about: The documentation assistant's four load profiles and their byte budgets (issue #481).
ONE table, two readers, on purpose. `scripts/check-docs-performance-budget.mjs` enforces
the profiles a built artifact can answer on its own (what a page references, how big an
artifact is, what a search costs). `packages/e2e/tests/docs/assistant-performance.e2e.ts`
enforces the SEQUENCING — that those bytes are fetched when a reader asks and not before —
which only a real browser can observe. Two tables would let the two drift, and the
sequencing test is the one that would quietly stop matching reality.
Every `maxBytes` below is a measured baseline plus stated headroom, not a guess. Raising one
is a reviewable one-line diff with a reason in `note`, which is the whole point of checking
the table in: a regression should have to be argued for, not merged silently.
Sizes are UNCOMPRESSED bytes on disk. Transfer size depends on the CDN's encoding and is not
reproducible in CI; on-disk bytes are, and they move in the same direction.

coldPage.label: 1. Cold documentation page (new or minimized reader)
description: Everything a reader downloads to read documentation with the assistant minimized: the
scripts and stylesheets a built page references, plus the corpus manifest.
The manifest belongs HERE rather than at first read. `docs-page-context.tsx` loads it on
every route so a navigation into a document resolves immediately instead of opening a
fresh `corpus_pending` window at exactly the moment a reader is most likely to ask
something — the design #474 and #476 locked. Issue #481's own text put the manifest at
profile 3; that wording predates the shipped design and was reconciled here.
This profile must NOT contain a runtime chunk. That is a separate, absolute rule enforced
by the eager-chunk check in the same script, not by a byte count.
coldPage.note: Measured 2026-08-02 at 842,987 bytes (825,563 of page-referenced JS/CSS — identical across all 31 built pages, since Docusaurus loads route chunks lazily — plus a 17,408-byte corpus manifest). ~19% headroom for ordinary Docusaurus/Infima growth; a jump here means a page started pulling something that should have stayed lazy.

assistantRuntime.label: 2. Opening the assistant
description: The incremental JavaScript fetched when a reader first activates the assistant — the
`assistant-runtime-client` chunk and everything webpack pulls with it (app-browser, the
agent runtime, the content platform).
Enforced from the browser rather than the build: which chunks activation actually pulls is
a property of webpack's chunk graph at runtime, and a static approximation of it would be
a number nobody could reproduce or trust.
This is a real cost, and it is the reader's choice to pay it — nothing here is downloaded
until they press the launcher, or unless they left the panel open last visit.
assistantRuntime.note: Measured 2026-08-02 at 2,605,410 bytes of JavaScript across a cold activation on Chromium, by the e2e spec that enforces this. ~23% headroom. It is a large number and an honest one: this is the whole product runtime, and it is why the profile is separate — a reader who never opens the assistant pays none of it. The spec prints the figure on every run, so a drift is visible before it is a breach.

documentRead.label: 3. First document read
description: One per-document corpus artifact — the normalized Markdown, outline, and section
boundaries for exactly the document a `read_doc`/`read_current_doc` selected.
Budgeted against the LARGEST artifact the site emits, so the number describes the worst
case a reader can actually hit rather than an average nobody experiences. Today that is
`plugins-and-tools/plugin-infrastructure.md`, the >54,000-character document #474's
balanced-overview rule was built around.
The guarantee that matters alongside the size is that only ONE of these is ever fetched.
That is the e2e spec's half.
documentRead.note: Measured 2026-08-02 at 62,363 bytes for `plugins-and-tools/plugin-infrastructure`, the largest of 28 emitted artifacts (the next is 38,849). ~60% headroom. A breach means either a document grew far beyond the rest or the artifact format started carrying something it should not.

search.label: 4. First search
description: The Lunr index and the private search worker, fetched only when `search_docs` runs.
Same index the documentation's own search bar uses — the adapter wraps the pinned
upstream worker rather than building a second index, so this profile is shared cost, not
additional cost, for a reader who also used the search bar.
Production-only by construction: the upstream plugin writes `search-index.json` from its
`postBuild` hook, so `docusaurus start` has none and the adapter reports
`index_dev_unsupported`. Finding the index here is therefore also the production-build
smoke check #481 asks for — if a build stops emitting it, this fails rather than the
assistant silently reporting search as unavailable in production.
TWO budgets, because there are two things to bound and only one of them is weighable from
the build. `maxBytes` is the index, which the build measures exactly.
`maxWorkerBytes` is the JavaScript fetched at the first search, which only a browser can
see — and which is only meaningful if the generic runtime is ALREADY WARM. The e2e spec
therefore performs an ordinary no-tool send before it starts measuring.
`maxWorkerBytes` also carries the LAZINESS assertion, and is why the spec requires it to
be greater than zero: if the search worker became an eager dependency of the assistant
runtime, nothing would arrive at first search and that floor would fail. The floor only
means that with the warm-up in place. Without it the measurement was dominated by the
first send's LiteLLM/ReAct chunks (~146 kB of the 192 kB originally recorded), so an eager
worker would have sailed past a floor of zero.
search.note: Measured 2026-08-02: 1,208,995 bytes for `search-index.json` (~49% headroom, wide because the index grows with the documentation), and 46,542 bytes of JavaScript at the first search on Chromium with the runtime warm (~50% headroom). That second figure was 192,027 before the warm-up isolated it — the difference was generic first-send machinery, not the search path.
